title: Constraints on type parameters
hook: Without a constraint, T is barely an object. with where, you can new it, compare it, treat it as an enum, or even allow a ref struct. Interviews expect the list, the exclusions, and the notnull warning.

sections.heading: The catalog
sections.prose: where T : class — T is a non-nullable reference type in an NRT context (class? allows nullable references). where T : struct — non-nullable value type; implies a parameterless constructor and cannot combine with new() or unmanaged. where T : new() — public parameterless constructor; must be last among ordinary constraints; cannot construct types that have required members. where T : notnull — non-nullable value or reference; violations warn, they do not error. where T : unmanaged — blittable non-nullable value type; implies struct. where T : Enum and where T : Delegate (or MulticastDelegate) are legal base constraints; they were CLR-legal long before C# allowed the syntax. where T : BaseType / IInterface and where T : U (naked type parameter) express inheritance. where T : default appears on overrides when the base method had neither class nor struct. allows ref struct is an anti-constraint: T may be a ref struct (Span<T>-like). It must come last, cannot mix with class, and is not inherited by other type parameters. Full Span rules stay in module 17; here you only need to know the clause exists so generic parsers can accept ReadOnlySpan<char>.

snippets.label: Constraints you actually write
snippets.explanation: IComparable unlocks CompareTo. new() unlocks new T(). Enum/Delegate are real constraints. notnull is a warning net. allows ref struct opts into ref-safety.

sections.heading: Order and conflicts
sections.prose: At most one of struct, class, class?, notnull, unmanaged — and that one is first. Base class cannot combine with those. new() cannot combine with struct or unmanaged. allows ref struct follows everything, including new(). Combining where T : class with == is a trap: == on T is reference identity even if T is string with an overloaded ==. Use IEquatable<T> when you mean value equality.

sections.heading: NRT interaction
sections.prose: In a nullable context, where T : class rejects string?. T? on an unconstrained T means “nullable if T is a reference, Nullable-like if T is a value.” That is why cache APIs prefer TryGet or MaybeNull over T? Get<T>(). The notnull constraint is how Dictionary keys stay honest with NRT.

interviewTakeaways: Constraints unlock operations on T; unbounded T is Object-like.
struct / unmanaged / new() have exclusion rules; new() last; allows ref struct last of all.
notnull warns; required members block new(); Enum and Delegate constraints are first-class.
commonPitfalls: Using == on a class-constrained T and expecting String overload behavior.
Expecting new() to work with required properties.

jsTsCorrelations.note: function f<T extends Foo>(x: T) is the TS analogue of where T : Foo. TS has no struct/unmanaged/ref struct story.
